cases.abstract: A larger context window does not establish that a language model can use evidence wherever it appears. We investigate this distinction through controlled tests of multi-document question answering and synthetic key-value retrieval, varying both context length and the location of the information needed for a fixed answer. Across the evaluated question-answering models, accuracy generally peaks at the beginning or end of the context and declines when the answer-bearing passage is in the middle. Extended-context versions do not consistently improve this pattern when the input also fits their shorter-context counterparts. The retrieval task exposes similar positional weaknesses in several models, although both evaluated Claude variants perform nearly perfectly. Repeating the query before and after the data largely resolves synthetic retrieval errors but leaves the question-answering pattern substantially unchanged. A complementary open-domain evaluation finds that reader accuracy levels off before retrieval recall, so additional documents often yield little benefit. These diagnostics distinguish accepting longer inputs from making effective use of them and show why exact-match retrieval improvements alone cannot establish better contextual question answering.
cases.methods: The evaluation changes evidence position without changing the required answer. For 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries with paragraph annotations, each input combines the annotated answer-bearing paragraph with retrieved Wikipedia distractors that exclude the annotated answers. Moving the answer-bearing document through contexts of 10, 20, or 30 documents measures positional sensitivity; adding distractors separately varies context length. Closed-book prompts establish performance without supplied evidence, while oracle prompts containing only the answer document indicate what models can achieve without distractor competition. A second task replaces natural-language documents with serialized JSON containing random UUID keys and values, testing retrieval with fewer semantic confounders. It uses 75, 140, or 300 pairs and 500 examples per setting. Both tasks use greedy decoding and score whether the correct answer or value appears in the output. These controls distinguish access to available information from nominal input capacity.
cases.results: Placing the query on both sides of the context produces a sharp contrast between token retrieval and question answering. With 300 key-value pairs, GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) reaches perfect retrieval accuracy, whereas its worst accuracy without this change is 45.6%. Yet the same intervention does not remove the positional pattern in multi-document question answering: it slightly helps when evidence comes first and slightly hurts other placements. This contrast shows that enabling documents to be processed with advance knowledge of the query can solve the synthetic matching task without solving evidence use in natural-language questions. Architecture comparisons further qualify the diagnosis. Flan-UL2 varies by only 1.9 percentage points within its 2,048-token training window, but develops a middle-position disadvantage on longer sequences. Context extensions also leave GPT-3.5-Turbo and its 16K counterpart nearly indistinguishable on shared-length inputs. The findings therefore support task- and training-length-dependent limitations, not a universal inability to retrieve from long contexts.
cases.notes: Prioritize controlled diagnosis over a remedy claim. Preserve Claude's retrieval exception, the shared-context condition for extended-model comparisons, and the distinction between synthetic retrieval and question answering. Architectural explanations remain hypotheses rather than identified causes. Avoid interpreting the source's ambiguous greater-than-20% drop as a specified percentage-point change.

cases.abstract: Retrieved passages can improve factual answers without ensuring that generated claims are supported by the passages cited. Self-RAG addresses this mismatch by training a language model to decide when retrieval is useful and to evaluate passage relevance, evidential support, and response utility through special reflection tokens. A separately trained critic supplies these annotations offline; the generator then learns text and reflection tokens together and performs its own evaluations at inference. When retrieval is triggered, sentence-level candidate continuations are ranked using their generation probabilities and reflection scores, allowing the balance between support and utility to change without retraining. Zero-shot task evaluations of trained 7B and 13B models cover factual question answering, classification, biographies, and cited long-form answers. Compared with a 7B baseline trained on the same instruction-output pairs and augmented with retrieval only at test time, Self-RAG improves PopQA accuracy from 48.7% to 54.9%. Its citation precision also exceeds retrieval-augmented ChatGPT on ASQA, although citation recall remains lower. Increasing the support weight improves precision at the expense of measured fluency, making controllable evidence use a trade-off rather than a guarantee of fully supported output.
cases.methods: Self-RAG makes retrieval and critique part of the generator's token prediction problem. A critic initialized from Llama 2-7B is trained on GPT-4 feedback, then annotates instruction-output pairs with retrieval decisions and judgments of relevance, support, and utility. These annotations and any retrieved passages form the generator's training examples. Standard next-token training teaches the generator to produce both response text and reflection tokens; retrieved passage tokens are excluded from the loss. At inference, a retrieval-token probability threshold determines whether external evidence is requested. For each sentence, the model can generate separate continuations conditioned on different retrieved passages, then use segment-level beam search to favor candidates with higher generation and critique scores. This operation evaluates support at the point where competing claims are selected, rather than treating retrieval alone as validation. Critique weights can be changed at test time, and the training critic is not needed during generation.
cases.results: The same-data comparison with Llama2-FT7B tests whether instruction-output pairs alone explain the gains. That baseline is fine-tuned without retrieval or reflection and receives retrieved passages only at test time. Self-RAG7B raises PopQA accuracy from 48.7% to 54.9% and ASQA citation precision from 5.0% to 66.9%, but ASQA correctness measured by str-em falls from 31.0% to 30.0%. Better attribution therefore does not imply improvement on every answer-quality metric. With the same ASQA input documents, Self-RAG13B also exceeds retrieval-augmented ChatGPT in citation precision, 70.3% versus 65.1%, while trailing in recall, 71.3% versus 76.6%, and str-em, 31.7% versus 40.7%. The inference controls expose another trade-off: emphasizing evidential support raises citation precision but reduces MAUVE, the reported fluency measure. Reducing retrieval frequency harms PopQA accuracy more than PubHealth accuracy. These comparisons support adjustable evidence selection and attribution, while showing that its costs depend on the task and output metric.
cases.notes: Use the table rather than blanket superiority wording: ASQA str-em and citation recall have unfavorable comparisons. The same-data baseline controls instruction-output pairs, not all training procedures. The 50k-instance ablations and 150-example ASQA subset are distinct from the 150k-instance main training setup; no ablation result is treated as full-test performance. Reflection tokens are learned judgments, not certificates.
